---
engine: markdown
title: "Bioinformatics (FASTA/FASTQ)"
---

Sequence files (`.fasta`, `.fa`, `.fna`, `.fastq`, `.fq`) are read and written
with [microseq](https://github.com/larssnip/microseq). A FASTA file becomes a
data frame with the columns `header` and `sequence`; a FASTQ file adds
`quality`.

## FASTA

Write a FASTA file from a data frame with `header` and `sequence` columns:

```{term}
rush run -o genes.fasta 'data.frame(
  header = c("gene1 E. coli", "gene2 B. subtilis", "gene3 S. aureus"),
  sequence = c("ATGAAACGCATTAGC", "ATGGCTTTAACGTTAGCCGTA", "ATGTCAGGT")
)'
cat genes.fasta
```

Read it, and compute on the sequences like any other column:

```{term}
rush run 'dplyr::mutate(df, length = nchar(sequence))' genes.fasta
```

Filter the sequences and write the result as FASTA again, here to standard
output with `-O fasta`:

```{term}
rush run -O fasta 'dplyr::filter(df, nchar(sequence) > 10)' genes.fasta
```

## FASTQ

A FASTQ file also stores the quality of each base:

```{term}
rush run -o reads.fastq 'data.frame(
  header = c("read1", "read2"),
  sequence = c("GATTACA", "ACGTTGCA"),
  quality = c("IIIIHHG", "IIIHHGGF")
)'
cat reads.fastq
```

```{term}
rush run 'df' reads.fastq
```

## Converting

Convert FASTQ to FASTA, which drops the quality:

```{term}
rush convert -o reads.fasta reads.fastq
cat reads.fasta
```

Or export sequences to CSV for other tools:

```{term}
rush convert -o genes.csv genes.fasta
cat genes.csv
```

```{term}
#| include: false
rm -f genes.fasta reads.fastq reads.fasta genes.csv
```
